appraisal_events.evidence: "C'est à quoi Eulalie excellait" — she alone can answer both "C'est la fin, ma pauvre Eulalie" and later reassure her; her Sunday visits are tante Léonie's one pleasure, and if her ring comes late "la faisait presque se trouver mal", while everyone else who failed the test was permanently barred.
appraisal_events.explanation: Eulalie is the sole visitor, besides the curé, who consistently satisfies tante Léonie's contradictory need for pity and reassurance, giving her a uniquely privileged and emotionally powerful place in the household that the narrator's account clearly endorses.

appraisal_events.evidence: Françoise "riait encore bien plus, comme d'un bon tour, des ruses toujours victorieuses de ma tante" and "au fond admirait sa maîtresse qu'elle jugeait supérieure à tous ces gens puisqu'elle ne voulait pas les recevoir."
appraisal_events.explanation: Françoise privately judges tante Léonie superior to the visitors she so effectively gets rid of, though the narrator's comic framing of the whole household ritual keeps this admiration at an ironic distance.

status_effects.explanation: Eulalie is one of only two people tante Léonie still receives, having passed a test that got every other visitor permanently barred.
Tante Léonie's week revolves around Eulalie's Sunday visit, to the point of near physical distress when she is late, giving Eulalie real leverage over her moods.
Léonie's anxious, almost desperate anticipation of Eulalie's visit shows her emotional dependence on Eulalie's flattering reassurance.

In Françoise's private estimation, tante Léonie's ever-successful stratagems for evicting unwanted visitors mark her as superior, though this is a private household judgment rather than a publicly registered one.
